description: Medieval toys, Victorian comics, BBC children's TV, video games and the decline of outdoor play.
content_html:
Medieval and Early Modern Children’s Play

Children’s play in medieval England was less clearly separated from adult activity than it is today. Young children had simple toys made from available materials: wooden horses and carts, clay figures, cloth dolls, and spinning tops. Archaeological excavations of medieval sites have recovered such objects, confirming that play was a recognised part of childhood. Children also participated in adult games and festivals from an early age.

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, toys became somewhat more elaborate but remained homemade or locally crafted. Hobby horses — simple wooden sticks with a carved horse’s head — were among the most common children’s playthings recorded in sources from this period. Boys played versions of football and wrestling alongside adults; girls were more typically directed towards domestic activities and needlework, though they too played with dolls and participated in communal games on feast days.

Key Fact

Victorian industrialisation transformed children’s toys. Factory-produced toys became available for the first time, including tin trains, mechanical toys, wooden building blocks and porcelain dolls. The introduction of compulsory education from 1870 and growing middle-class prosperity drove demand for educational and recreational toys. Wealthy children could afford elaborate toy trains and dolls’ houses; poorer children still made do with homemade objects.

Victorian and Edwardian Comics

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw the development of illustrated magazines and comics aimed at children. The comics industry grew alongside mass literacy, as the Education Act of 1870 brought compulsory schooling for all children. Comics offered affordable weekly entertainment: titles aimed at boys typically featured adventure, sport and humour, while girls’ comics emphasised friendship, home and romance.

The Beano launched in 1938 and the Dandy in 1937 — both published by D.C. Thomson in Dundee — became the most enduring British children’s comics of the twentieth century. The Eagle, launched in 1950 by clergyman Marcus Morris, targeted older boys with its distinctive combination of science fiction (Dan Dare, Pilot of the Future), adventure strips and educational content. At its peak in the 1950s, the Eagle sold nearly a million copies a week.

BBC radio provided dedicated children’s programming from its early years. Children’s Hour, first broadcast in 1922, offered stories, drama and music for younger listeners, and ran until 1961. Listen with Mother, aimed at the youngest children, ran from 1950 to 1982. When television reached British homes in the 1950s, children’s programming transferred quickly to the new medium.

Blue Peter launched on the BBC in October 1958 and has run continuously since, making it one of the longest-running children’s television programmes in the world. Watch with Mother (1950–1980) served pre-school children with puppet programmes including The Flowerpot Men and The Wooden Tops. Children’s television became a significant part of the BBC’s public service remit, providing programming that was both entertaining and educational.

The Video Game Revolution

The late twentieth century saw a new form of children’s entertainment that was interactive in a way no previous medium had been. Video games arrived in British homes with the Atari 2600 in the late 1970s and the rise of home computers such as the ZX Spectrum (1982) and the Commodore 64 (1982). Nintendo’s Game Boy (1989) and its console systems brought new levels of sophistication; the Sony PlayStation (1995) and its successors brought cinematic-quality graphics.

By the early 2000s, video games had become the dominant leisure activity for many children and teenagers. The industry’s global revenue surpassed that of cinema by the early twenty-first century. Games also changed the nature of play: it became more solitary and screen-based, and it extended into adulthood in a way that traditional children’s toys did not.

One of the most significant changes in children’s leisure from the late twentieth century was the decline of outdoor, unsupervised play. In the 1970s, a typical British child walked or cycled to school, played freely in the street or on waste ground, and ranged relatively widely without adult supervision. By the 2000s, parental fears about road traffic and stranger danger had dramatically reduced this freedom. Research by Play England found that children’s “home range” — the area within which they were allowed to roam freely — had shrunk by approximately 90% between the 1970s and the 2000s.

Key Fact

By the start of the twenty-first century, children’s leisure had shifted decisively from outdoor, unsupervised, physical play to indoor, screen-based, often solitary activities. This represented a radical break with centuries of tradition, in which children’s play had been primarily communal, physical and outdoor. The change was driven by technology, rising parental anxiety, traffic, and the entertainment industry’s targeting of children as consumers.
exam_tip_html: Children’s entertainment questions invite you to trace a very long sweep of change, from medieval toys to video games. Be precise about the timing and cause of each shift. For example, the Victorian toy industry grew because of industrialisation and the 1870 Education Act (mass literacy); the video game industry grew because of microchip technology. For a 16-mark thematic change essay, you must address whether change was gradual or rapid, and weigh it against continuity (some elements of children’s play, like role-play and storytelling, have persisted for centuries).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval children played with simple handmade toys; Victorian industrialisation produced factory-made toys alongside a comics industry driven by mass literacy after the 1870 Education Act.
  • BBC children’s radio (from 1922) and television (Blue Peter from 1958) made broadcasting a central part of children’s leisure; video games from the late 1970s onwards created a new interactive entertainment medium.
  • By the early twenty-first century, outdoor unsupervised play had declined sharply, with screen-based leisure dominating children’s free time — a fundamental break with centuries of communal, physical play.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of children's play in the medieval period.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. children played with simple toys made from wood, clay, leather or cloth, such as hobby horses or clay figures / children participated in adult games and festivals from an early age. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of children's comics in the twentieth century.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. the Beano (1938) and Dandy (1937) became the most enduring British children's comics, published weekly by D.C. Thomson (feature + detail); the Eagle (1950) targeted older boys with science fiction and adventure, selling nearly a million copies a week at its peak in the 1950s (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Victorian toys became more varied and commercially produced compared with medieval toys.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking industrialisation (factory production making toys cheaper and more varied), growing middle-class prosperity and the 1870 Education Act driving literacy and demand for educational toys. Evidence-based. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the decline of outdoor play for children in Britain by the early twenty-first century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. children's home range shrank by approximately 90% between the 1970s and 2000s; reduced physical activity has been linked to health concerns; loss of unsupervised communal play changed child development and social bonding patterns. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant was the development of television in changing how children spent their leisure time in the second half of the twentieth century?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses television's significance at the time (Blue Peter from 1958, Watch with Mother, children's BBC as public service remit) AND over time (laid the basis for screen-based leisure that video games and streaming extended). Uses evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Children's leisure became less physical and less communal between c.500 and the present day.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substantiated judgement tracing change across all three eras. Agrees: screen-based, solitary video games contrast with medieval communal play; decline of outdoor play. Challenges: children's sports still flourish; gaming can be social and online; continuity in storytelling and role-play. Overall weighing conclusion. Secure: Evidence from at least two eras, some weighing. Developing: Limited range. Emerging: Basic agree/disagree. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What were the Beano and Dandy, and when did they first launch?
options: BBC children's radio programmes launched in the 1920s
Long-running illustrated comics launched in 1937 and 1938 by D.C. Thomson
Children's television programmes launched in the 1950s
Victorian illustrated books aimed at middle-class children

knowledge_checks.q: What game console first brought video games to British homes in the late 1970s?
Blue Peter, the long-running BBC children's television programme, was first broadcast in _____.
Children's home range — the area within which they could roam freely — shrank by approximately _____% between the 1970s and the 2000s.
Match each form of children's entertainment to its era or description:
right: Simple wooden stick-and-head toys common among children in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries
1950s comic targeting older boys with science fiction stories, selling nearly a million copies weekly
Interactive electronic leisure introduced to British homes from the late 1970s

flashcard_questions.q: What were common medieval children's toys made from?
flashcard_questions.a: Wood, clay, leather or cloth — typically crafted by parents or local craftspeople.
Simple wooden sticks with a carved horse's head, one of the most common children's toys in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Eagle comic, and when did it launch?
flashcard_questions.a: A 1950 boys' comic featuring Dan Dare and adventure strips, selling nearly a million copies a week at its peak.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Blue Peter, and when did it first broadcast?
flashcard_questions.a: A long-running BBC children's magazine programme, first broadcast in October 1958.
A BBC radio programme aimed at young children, broadcast 1950 to 1982.
Electronic games requiring active player input, played on consoles or computers.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Sony PlayStation launch?
What has research shown about children's home range between the 1970s and 2000s?
flashcard_questions.a: It shrank by approximately 90% — children were allowed to roam far less freely.

flashcard_questions.q: What drove the growth of the Victorian toy industry?
flashcard_questions.a: Industrialisation making factory-made toys affordable, and the 1870 Education Act driving mass literacy and demand.

glossary_terms.definition: Objects made for children to play with, in the medieval period typically crafted from wood, clay, leather or cloth by parents or local craftspeople.
Illustrated periodicals aimed at children and teenagers, featuring comic strips, adventure stories and humour.
A long-running BBC children's television programme first broadcast in 1958, known for its magazine format, pets and make-and-do activities.
Electronic games played on dedicated consoles, computers or handheld devices, requiring active player input rather than passive consumption.
